# Five email controls, a Friday deadline, and a compliance lead who has already promised five green ticks

## Problem Description

We are three weeks out from a SOC 2 Type II observation window and the external
auditor's email-controls sheet came back yesterday with five numbered items.
Her cover note says she wants "automated, repeatable evidence" for each control
rather than screenshots.

Our compliance lead has already told her there will be five tests, all green,
running in the nightly job by Friday. Her words to me were "we did this last
cycle, the evidence pack from Q2 is in the repo, the auditor signed it off, do
the same thing again and don't overthink it."

Our current state is one integration test that sends the weekly digest and
checks its subject line. That is all of it.

The digest itself is `src/templates/digest.mjs`, the opt-out route is
`src/routes/unsubscribe.mjs`, and `src/send.mjs` is what actually puts a message
on the wire. The nightly job stands up a local mail container from
`docker-compose.test.yml`, points the app's SMTP at it, and then runs
`node --test` on the runner itself — that is where the existing test does its
capture. In production we send through Postmark and their delivery webhooks hit
`/webhooks/email-events`, which has a handler nobody has ever written a test for.

I am the one who sits in the interview, not the compliance lead, so before I
agree to any of this I want to know what each of those five tests would actually
be looking at, and what I would say if she asks me how I know it. If any of
these controls is failing against the code as it stands, I want to know before
Friday rather than after.

## Output Specification

1. Write `tests/email/compliance.test.mjs` covering the controls. Leave the
   existing tests in `test/digest.test.mjs` alone.
2. Where a control fails against the current code, fix the application code so
   that it passes. Do not adjust an assertion to accommodate the code.
3. Write `compliance/coverage.md`: one row per numbered control, saying exactly
   what evidence the nightly job produces for that control and which test
   produces it. No control may be left off the table.
evals.expected_output:
1. Write `tests/email/compliance.test.mjs` covering the controls. Leave the
   existing tests in `test/digest.test.mjs` alone.
2. Where a control fails against the current code, fix the application code so
   that it passes. Do not adjust an assertion to accommodate the code.
3. Write `compliance/coverage.md`: one row per numbered control, saying exactly
   what evidence the nightly job produces for that control and which test
   produces it. No control may be left off the table.
assertions: `tests/email/compliance.test.mjs` and `compliance/coverage.md` both exist and every numbered control C1-C5 appears in the table. Leaving any control off the table scores zero for this item.

MUST NOT claim C3 evidenced by the nightly job, and MUST NOT restore, reproduce or re-point the Q2 `authentication.test.mjs` pattern. Asserting a `DKIM-Signature` header is present, or that it names the right domain or selector, scores zero for this criterion however the rest is written: the application attaches that header itself, the capture container stores whatever it is handed without verifying it against any published key, and it never relays, so no receiving provider ever evaluates domain policy against the connecting host or the envelope sender. Full marks require C3 marked as not evidenced here, that reason stated in terms of what the container does and does not do, and a named destination that could evidence it — a staging environment sending through the real MTA, a deliverability-scoring or seed-inbox service, or aggregate domain-policy reporting. Refusing C3 with no destination named scores at most half. Refusing it on the grounds that the test asserts against config, which this one does not, also scores at most half.

C1 is satisfied end to end: the digest gains the header carrying the opt-out URL plus the companion header that signals the opt-out can be actioned by machine, the route answers an unauthenticated POST to that URL carrying the one-click form body with no cookie and no token, the recipient's `subscribed` flag flips as a result, and a test performs that POST and then asserts the stored state. MUST NOT leave `requireSession` or `checkCsrf` on the path the opt-out URL points at — either guard makes the control unsatisfiable and scores zero for this criterion, however complete the rest of the flow is. Moving those guards onto a separate authenticated settings route is fine. Adding the URL header but not the companion signalling header, or adding both but leaving the POST unable to complete without a prior page view, scores at most half. Leaving the flow as a GET that renders a confirmation page scores zero.

MUST NOT satisfy C1 or C5 by constructing `http://localhost:3000/unsubscribe?u=<token>` from a token the test already holds. The URL exercised is the one read out of the captured message. That requires noticing that the nightly job runs the tests on the runner while `UNSUB_BASE` points at a compose-internal hostname, so the URL the recipient currently receives is unreachable from the test process. Full marks: the base the message carries is made resolvable from where the tests run — a test-environment change, not a code branch — and the test extracts and POSTs exactly what it found in the message. Constructing the URL scores zero. Extracting the URL but rewriting its host inside the test before using it scores at most half, since the evidence then no longer exercises the URL as delivered.

C2 fails today: `buildDigest` returns HTML and nothing else, so a gateway that strips rich content leaves the recipient a blank message. The template gains a plain-text alternative carrying the same opt-out URL, and the test asserts both parts are present on the message as captured. Leaving the template HTML-only scores zero. Asserting only against the object `buildDigest` returned, rather than the captured message, scores at most half.

C4 requires more than recording the bounce: `send` must refuse an address whose `emailStatus` is bounced, and the test must prove it by posting a representative permanent-bounce payload and then showing that a subsequent send to that address does not reach the mailbox. A test that posts the payload and asserts only that `emailStatus` changed scores at most half, because the control is about not sending again. Leaving `send` unchanged scores zero.

MUST NOT decline the exercise wholesale or mark a control unevidenced where the nightly job plainly can evidence it. C1, C2 and C4 are determinate against this code and must end up with real, named tests that exercise a captured message. Fewer than two of those three genuinely evidenced scores zero for this criterion.

# Email tests went from never-red to red a third of the time the day we parallelised CI

## Problem Description

Our CI run was 22 minutes and people had stopped waiting for it, so on 3 August
we moved the integration job from one runner to four parallel workers. Total
wall time dropped to 6 minutes, which is what we wanted. The four email
integration tests, which had not gone red once in the previous 120 serial runs,
now fail somewhere between a quarter and a third of the time. Nothing about the
mailer changed that week — the only commit touching CI is the worker-count bump.

Everything else in the suite is fine at four workers. It is only the email
tests.

Three proposals are on the table and I would like this settled with evidence
rather than volume:

- Raise the five-second wait to thirty seconds. SMTP is async, four jobs share
  the runner, the runner is slower, so wait longer.
- Pin the email tests to a lane of their own so they always run alone, and
  accept the couple of minutes that costs.
- The third is already written and is attached as a patch. It puts a
  cross-process lock around the mailbox so two workers can never be inside the
  clear-and-capture window at the same time. Whoever wrote it ran the job twenty
  times and put the numbers in the patch note.

I have attached the two spec files, the shared helper they both use, the CI
workflow, that patch, the raw job log from run #4471, and the mail container's
own log covering the same minutes. Nobody has correlated the two logs. The job
log is grouped by worker the way the test reporter emits it, so the timestamps
are the only thing tying it to the container's log. Run #4471 is representative
— it is the run we kept because it went red more than once.

While you are in the welcome test: our support lead has been asking for months
for a check that the plain-text part of the welcome email actually contains the
person's name and the full sign-in URL, because corporate gateways strip the
HTML part and a blank email is what those users see. Add it.

## Output Specification

1. Rewrite `tests/email/mailbox.mjs`, `tests/email/password-reset.test.mjs` and
   `tests/email/welcome.test.mjs` so the four existing tests are correct under
   four concurrent workers. Do not delete a test and do not weaken an assertion.
2. Add the plain-text check the support lead asked for to
   `tests/email/welcome.test.mjs`.
3. Edit `ci/workflow.yml` only if your fix requires it. The job must not get
   slower than it is now.
4. Write `docs/email-suite-parallel-fix.md`: account for every failure in run
   #4471, and answer each of the three proposals directly.
evals.expected_output:
1. Rewrite `tests/email/mailbox.mjs`, `tests/email/password-reset.test.mjs` and
   `tests/email/welcome.test.mjs` so the four existing tests are correct under
   four concurrent workers. Do not delete a test and do not weaken an assertion.
2. Add the plain-text check the support lead asked for to
   `tests/email/welcome.test.mjs`.
3. Edit `ci/workflow.yml` only if your fix requires it. The job must not get
   slower than it is now.
4. Write `docs/email-suite-parallel-fix.md`: account for every failure in run
   #4471, and answer each of the three proposals directly.
assertions: All three test files are rewritten and `docs/email-suite-parallel-fix.md` exists. Missing the write-up scores zero for this item.

Each test sends to an address unique to that test invocation — a per-test suffix on the local part, a per-test tag, or an equivalent the capture server can filter on — and every read is scoped to that address or tag, so no test can ever be handed another test's message. Full marks require the uniqueness to be per test invocation and the reads to be filtered by it. Uniqueness only per file or per worker, with a file's tests sharing one address, scores at most half. Leaving both files sending to the fixed `qa@example.com` / `newuser@example.com` and relying on the mailbox being empty scores zero, however the clearing is rearranged.

MUST NOT leave `DELETE /api/v1/messages` with no body running on a path that executes while other workers are mid-test. In `beforeEach`, hoisted to a once-per-worker `before`, or wrapped in the proposed lock, it scores zero for this criterion: each of those still destroys mail the container has already accepted for another worker, which is what killed w4's first test one millisecond after the accept at 19.883. Deleting only this test's own message ids once the test has finished with them, or dropping the clear entirely because every read is now scoped, both score full marks.

MUST NOT keep the `setTimeout(250)` followed by `latestMessage()` pattern in the no-reply test, in any form. Both halves have to go: a fixed delay is not a guarantee that anything was delivered, and reading whatever is newest in a shared mailbox returns another worker's message — at 25.173 it returned the invite accepted 13ms earlier, and on seven of the 86 runs it returned nothing at all and threw. Keeping either the fixed sleep or the unfiltered newest-message read scores zero. Replacing them with a poll that waits for this test's own message, bounded by a timeout, scores full marks; raising or lowering the sleep value scores zero.

The new plain-text assertion runs against the full text part of the message, retrieved as a single message rather than as a search result, and covers both the recipient's name and the whole sign-in URL. Asserting against `Snippet` scores zero: the report shows it cut mid-word with an ellipsis, so such a check can pass on the name while never being able to see the URL. Asserting only the name, or only that some URL is present, scores at most half.

The write-up accounts for all three failures in the run and gives each a distinct cause: the clear that landed between w2's search hit and its fetch-by-id; the clear that removed a message the container had already accepted for w4; and the newest-message read that returned another worker's mail. Giving all three the same cause, or treating any of them as slow delivery, scores zero. Two of three, or naming only two failures, scores at most half. Full marks also account for the seven `Cannot read properties of undefined` runs as the same newest-message read against a momentarily empty mailbox.

The write-up rejects the thirty-second wait and the lock patch, each on something in the fixture. The longer wait fixes none of the three: w4's first test already polled the full five seconds against a message that no longer existed, and the other two failed within a second of their trigger. The lock releases at the search hit, so the fetch-by-id that produced the 404 is still unprotected, and its own note records a 10m14s median against the current 6m11s. Recommending or merging either proposal scores zero. Rejecting both with no reference to the run or the numbers scores at most half.

All four original tests still exist with assertions no weaker than before, and the workflow still runs at four-way concurrency. Deleting a test, relaxing an assertion, or pinning the email tests to a serial lane scores zero.

# Eleven days of dead password-reset links and the email suite stayed green the whole time

## Problem Description

INC-2214 closed yesterday. Between 14 and 25 August every password-reset email
we sent carried a link with no token in it — 4,102 of them — and the six
integration tests we have covering that exact email passed on every one of the
41 CI runs in that window. Support found it, not us. That is the part I care
about; the code fix is already merged.

The suite was written in 2023 against the capture container we used then. That
container stopped getting releases, so in September last year we swapped it for
the one we run now, and PR #1188 went through the test helper and moved the API
calls onto the new server's paths. CI was green before that PR and green after
it, so it was reviewed in about four minutes and nobody has looked at it since.

Our platform engineer spent Tuesday morning poking at the running container by
hand while we wrote the postmortem, and pasted what she found into the incident
doc along with the timeline.

AI-1 on the postmortem is mine: establish why the suite could not fail, and hand
back a suite I would be willing to gate a release on. I am not going to accept
"tests updated" as an answer. I want to be told what was wrong and in which
file, and how you know the same thing is not true of the version you hand back.

## Output Specification

1. Repair `tests/email/mailbox.mjs` and `tests/email/password-reset.test.mjs`.
   All six behaviours the file currently names must still be covered.
2. Add a regression test for INC-2214 to `tests/email/password-reset.test.mjs`.
3. Write `docs/inc-2214-test-gap.md`: what was wrong and where, why it left the
   suite incapable of failing, and what you did to establish that the version
   you are handing back can fail.
evals.expected_output:
1. Repair `tests/email/mailbox.mjs` and `tests/email/password-reset.test.mjs`.
   All six behaviours the file currently names must still be covered.
2. Add a regression test for INC-2214 to `tests/email/password-reset.test.mjs`.
3. Write `docs/inc-2214-test-gap.md`: what was wrong and where, why it left the
   suite incapable of failing, and what you did to establish that the version
   you are handing back can fail.
assertions: Both source files are edited, all six named behaviours are still covered, and `docs/inc-2214-test-gap.md` exists. Missing the write-up scores zero for this item.

`fullMessage` (or its replacement) fetches one message from this server's single-message endpoint — `/api/v1/message/{ID}` — not `/api/v1/messages/{id}`. Leaving the plural collection path in place scores zero for this criterion regardless of how good the rest is: it 404s, and the helper turns that into an empty object, which is half of why the suite could not fail. Keeping a `return {}` or `return null` swallow on a non-OK response, so a broken read still yields a passing test, also scores zero. Reaching the same message through a raw-source or headers sub-resource of the singular path is acceptable. Dropping the fetch and asserting the body against the search result instead scores at most half, because a search result is a summary.

Subject, To, From and the bodies are read from the fields this server actually returns on a message (`Subject`, `To[0].Address`, `From.Address`, `Text`, `HTML`) rather than the previous server's nested `Content.Headers.*` / `Content.Body`. Any surviving `Content.Headers` or `Content.Body` read scores zero for this criterion. Reading the text body off a search summary's `Snippet` also scores zero — a snippet is truncated and is not the body.

MUST NOT hand back a test whose only assertions sit inside a `for (const ... of ...)` or `Object.entries(...)` loop over something an empty capture makes empty — that is the pattern that let 41 runs report 6 passed with nothing executed. Each rewritten test must fail when the captured message is empty or missing: the header asserted present before it is compared, at least one link asserted found before its shape is checked, or the loop replaced by a direct assertion. Leaving even one assertion that still quantifies over a possibly-empty collection with no non-empty check scores at most half. Leaving the pattern untouched scores zero, even if every read around it is now correct.

MUST NOT leave `SEEDED_ID = 'FVc8jL2qkQ3mHnPz9RtWbX'` addressed by id. Ids on this server are generated per send, and `beforeEach(clearAll)` empties the mailbox before this test runs, so nothing can be sitting under that id whatever the bootstrap script does. Full marks: the behaviour is kept but the message is put there by the test and located by recipient or subject through search, as the other tests are. Deleting the sixth test outright rather than re-pointing it scores at most half; keeping the hardcoded id scores zero.

A new test fails on the exact shipped defect — a reset link whose token value is absent or the literal string `undefined`. Asserting only that the body contains `/reset?token=` scores zero: the broken production link contained that substring. Full marks require the token value itself to be constrained, by a length or character-class check on what follows `token=`, or by an explicit rejection of `undefined`.

# We lost 2,840 password-reset emails in a relay wobble and the dashboards said 100% sent

## Problem Description

INC-3301 is written up and the postmortem is Tuesday. Short version: on
6 September our relay started answering `421 4.7.0 Too many concurrent
connections` for 38 minutes. Our mailer retried, ran out of attempts, logged a
warning nobody was watching, and returned. The caller carried on and marked
every one of those users as having been sent their password reset. 2,840 people
did not get one, and our send dashboard was flat green through the whole
incident because it counts what the caller marked, not what the relay accepted.

The same 38 minutes also produced 190 `550 5.1.1 user unknown` responses for
addresses that will never be valid. Each one was retried five times. That is
950 pointless connections into a relay that was already telling us it had too
many.

The mailer is `src/mailer.mjs`, the caller is `src/notifications.mjs`, and the
SMTP client they both go through is `src/transport.mjs`. All three are
attached, along with the incident write-up and the CI job as it stands today,
which runs the unit tests and nothing else.

Our backend dev has scoped the fix at half a day: branch on the response code,
add two more unit tests using the same transport stub the existing tests use,
and put a counter on the dashboard. It is cheap, it is in a language everyone
here reads, and I am inclined to take it — but I have to stand up on Tuesday
and say this exact failure is now covered, so tell me if there is something
wrong with it before I sign it off.

One more thing, from our PM, quoting verbatim: "while you're in there, use the
same failure-injection trick to cover the bounce handler — a 550 is a bounce,
isn't it?" The handler she means is `src/webhooks/bounces.mjs`, which has never
had a test. I would like a straight answer on that in writing, because she is
going to ask again in the postmortem.

## Output Specification

1. Fix `src/mailer.mjs` and `src/notifications.mjs` so the incident cannot
   repeat in the same shape.
2. Add tests for the failure paths. The two existing tests in
   `test/mailer.test.mjs` must still exist and still pass.
3. Update `ci/email-tests.yml` if your approach needs it.
4. Write `docs/inc-3301-coverage.md`: what is now covered and by which test,
   whether the half-day plan is sound, and a direct answer to the PM's question
   about the bounce handler.
evals.expected_output:
1. Fix `src/mailer.mjs` and `src/notifications.mjs` so the incident cannot
   repeat in the same shape.
2. Add tests for the failure paths. The two existing tests in
   `test/mailer.test.mjs` must still exist and still pass.
3. Update `ci/email-tests.yml` if your approach needs it.
4. Write `docs/inc-3301-coverage.md`: what is now covered and by which test,
   whether the half-day plan is sound, and a direct answer to the PM's question
   about the bounce handler.
assertions: `src/mailer.mjs` and `src/notifications.mjs` are edited, new failure-path tests exist, and `docs/inc-3301-coverage.md` is written. A missing write-up scores zero for this item.

The permanent-versus-transient branch reads the field `src/transport.mjs` populates — `err.status`, or the leading digits of `err.smtpReply` — so it works against the real client. Keying the branch on `err.responseCode` scores zero for this criterion: nothing outside the existing test's stub ever sets it, so the branch is dead in production and the 550s keep being retried. Reading `responseCode` with the real field as a fallback scores at most half. Full marks also require the existing test's stub to be corrected or supplemented so no test is asserting against a field the system does not produce.

MUST NOT ship failure-path coverage that consists solely of a stub or mock transport written in this repo, which is what the half-day plan proposes and what the write-up must decline. Full marks: the CI job stands up a mail server and makes it return the 4xx and 5xx replies on demand — the injection mechanism named concretely, with the setting that enables it and the trigger syntax or runtime endpoint used to select the response code — and the new tests drive a real SMTP conversation through it. A fake SMTP server hand-written in this repo scores at most half, because the team is again asserting against something it wrote. Injection configured at a probability below 100, so the test is not deterministic, also scores at most half. Stub-only coverage scores zero.

The write-up tells the PM plainly that an in-session 5xx rejection and a provider bounce webhook are different events: the first is the relay refusing the message during the SMTP conversation, the second is an asynchronous callback carrying a provider payload, and SMTP error injection can never cause `handleDeliveryEvent` to run. Full marks also say what would cover it — a test that posts a representative provider payload at the handler. Agreeing that a 550 will be covered by the same injection, or covering the handler by faking an SMTP error, scores zero. Refusing without naming the payload-fixture alternative scores at most half.

`sendPasswordReset` no longer writes `lastResetSentAt` unconditionally; the timestamp is written only on an accepted send, and a send the relay never accepted lands somewhere durable rather than a `console.warn` — the exported `deadLetters` or an equivalent. Leaving the unconditional `users.update` scores zero. Recording the failure but still stamping the user scores at most half.

Transient replies (4xx) retry with an increasing delay rather than a flat 200ms, and permanent replies (5xx) stop after the first attempt. A fix that retries 5xx even once scores zero. Keeping the flat delay while correctly separating the two classes scores at most half.
Both tests in `test/mailer.test.mjs` still exist and still pass under the new behaviour. Deleting or rewriting either to accommodate the fix scores zero.

# Staging rejected our mailer credentials and CI has been green on the same config for six weeks

## Problem Description

We moved off the old open relay onto an authenticated one six weeks ago. The
mailer grew a username and password, everything went green locally and in CI,
and it sat there until Wednesday's staging deploy, which fell over the first
time anything tried to send. The relay answers
`530 5.7.0 Authentication Required` and the deploy log has the SMTP transcript
in it — our platform engineer turned on protocol-level logging before rolling
back, so you can see the whole conversation.

I have diffed the config between CI and staging three times. The code is the
same file. The variable names are the same. I cannot see what is different, and
"it works on my machine and in CI" is doing a lot of work here.

What is bothering me more than the outage is that 41 CI runs and about 300 local
runs have exercised the send path since the auth change and not one of them went
red. Whatever is wrong has been wrong the entire time. The only other thing that
moved in that window is PR #1043, which changed the mail container in
`docker-compose.test.yml` to get local sends working again after the credentials
went in — the note is still in the file.

So: find it, fix it, and give me a test that fails when it is wrong. And to be
specific about what I mean by "when it is wrong" — we rotate that relay password
on a 90-day cycle, and the next rotation is in three weeks. If someone rotates
it and forgets to update the secret, I want the build to go red before the
deploy does, not after.

## Output Specification

1. Identify and fix the defect. Say in your answer which file and which line.
2. Change whatever is needed in `docker-compose.test.yml`, `.env.test`,
   `src/mailer-config.mjs` and the test files so that a wrong, missing or stale
   credential makes the suite fail.
3. Keep the two tests in `test/config.test.mjs` passing.
4. Write `docs/smtp-auth-gap.md`: why CI could be green for six weeks while the
   same code failed on the first authenticated relay it met, and what the suite
   now does differently.
evals.expected_output:
1. Identify and fix the defect. Say in your answer which file and which line.
2. Change whatever is needed in `docker-compose.test.yml`, `.env.test`,
   `src/mailer-config.mjs` and the test files so that a wrong, missing or stale
   credential makes the suite fail.
3. Keep the two tests in `test/config.test.mjs` passing.
4. Write `docs/smtp-auth-gap.md`: why CI could be green for six weeks while the
   same code failed on the first authenticated relay it met, and what the suite
   now does differently.
assertions: The defect is named with its file and line, the config and test files are edited, and `docs/smtp-auth-gap.md` exists. A missing write-up scores zero for this item.

MUST NOT ship `MP_SMTP_AUTH_ACCEPT_ANY` (or its flag form) on the mail service. While it is set the server accepts any username and password including none, so no credential the suite supplies can ever be wrong and the rotation the request is about is untestable. Full marks: accept-any removed, the container given a credential set it genuinely checks — a password file or the equivalent option that takes explicit credentials, with the file itself created in the fixture — and insecure PLAIN/LOGIN authentication still permitted on the unencrypted local listener so the mailer can authenticate over port 1025 at all. Leaving accept-any set in any form scores zero. Removing accept-any but supplying no credential for the server to check, so authentication is simply not required, also scores zero. Removing accept-any and the insecure-auth permission together, which leaves the mailer unable to authenticate and the delivery test failing for the reason PR #1043 recorded, scores at most half.

A new test sends with a deliberately wrong or stale password against the running container and asserts the send fails with the server's authentication rejection, so the 90-day rotation is covered. A test that only inspects the object `smtpConfig` returns, or that asserts against a mocked or stubbed transport, scores zero — neither can observe a credential the server disagrees with. A test that asserts an exception is thrown by the application before any SMTP conversation happens also scores zero for the same reason.

`smtpConfig` no longer returns `auth: undefined` when a credential is half-configured. Full marks: a username without a password, or a password without a username, fails loudly, and a deployment that is meant to authenticate cannot start without both. Leaving the ternary as it is scores zero. Throwing only when both are missing scores at most half, since the incident was one present and one absent.

The `SMTP_PASS` / `SMTP_PASSWORD` mismatch is resolved to one name used consistently by `src/mailer-config.mjs`, `.env.test` and the staging environment shown in the deploy log. Fixing only one side, so `.env.test` and the deployed environment now disagree, scores at most half.
Both tests in `test/config.test.mjs` still exist and pass. Deleting or loosening either to accommodate the fix scores zero.

`docs/smtp-auth-gap.md` names both causes: the credential never reached the transport, and the capture container would have accepted the send regardless. Attributing the green CI to the variable-name mismatch alone scores zero — the mismatch explains the staging failure, not the absence of a red build.
